Industry News: "Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.
  • Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for newly introduced designs: the finds from archaeological digs.
  • However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.

Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for newly introduced designs: the finds from archaeological digs.

However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.

Deselected finds are duplicates, common in type, poorly preserved or otherwise judged to have limited future research value.

According to recent reports, “The material that you see here is the lowest of the lowest quality,” mentioned Isarin at a preview of Ex Situ at this year’s Dutch Design Week. “It’s not preserved. It doesn’t belong in a museum. It doesn’t belong in a depot.”.

In fact, if it is not going to be used for educational purposes or reference collections, deselected archaeological finds are required by Dutch law to be carefully destroyed, as they are in many places around the world, said Isarin and Klaster.

Although the materials may be of low value to archaeology, the designers both found this something of a waste. With Ex Situ, they aim to explore a new category of use and preservation for these materials, believing artists and designers have the capacity to tell stories of heritage in a different way to museums.

With the permission of the province of South Holland, they gave deselected materials to nine Dutch practitioners with expertise in crafts such as ceramics, woodwork and glassmaking.

One of the most finished pieces, exhibited in a preview showcase at October’s Dutch Design Week in the Klokgebouw, was by footwear designer and materials researcher Judith Sanders.

She crafted the foundation posts from a section of the Roman Limes border road, dated to 125AD and built under the emperor Hadrian, into the heel of a pair of high-heeled shoes. Sanders was intrigued by the notion that they could perform structurally once again – this time bearing the load of just one person.

Bold numbers on the sides of the shoe denote where on the dig site the material came from, while a second pair of shoes works leather from the middle ages into a modern-day sneaker silhouette.

Another piece is by designer-maker Daan Simons, who worked with 14th-century wood fragments from a ship that was wrecked and then subsequently used in the construction of Rotterdam.

The texture and existing peg holes in the wood are preserved in his Remembrance Pots, which he imagines holding the ashes of a loved one or a keepsake of theirs, compounding the layers of memory in the vessel.

Klaster and Isarin started on the path to Ex Situ after meeting accidentally at their timber drying kiln, where she was having some wood dried for a furniture project, and he was having the deselected Roman posts dried in the hope they would find another life.

Industry observers note that “Intrigued by their blackness”, Klaster asked Isarin if she could have them, and went on to make a series of tall vases. That was five years ago, and they have been discussing the potential intersection of archaeology and design ever since.

Klaster indicates that the Ex Situ designers were supported with information about heritage and the finds they were working with, but that the project naturally inspired some trepidation.

In a recent development, “In the work that they have made so far, you see that they have thought it through, and there is respect in what they made,” said Klaster. “But the first cut with a scissor or a bandsaw is, of course, a scary thing.”.

Recent findings suggest that “[One of the designers] was like, can I really saw that in two? And I mentioned yes, you can. If you have a strategy as a designer, yes, it’s yours.”.

That worry will be echoed among some archaeologists, Isarin adds, and he and Klaster’s aim is for the exhibition to promote discussion among the profession.

Industry observers note that “For archaeologists, this material is in a sense sacred,” mentioned Isarin. “But it’s deselected, so nobody wants it.”.

He said that while reactions have so far been positive, the issue becomes more thorny if the design were to take place in a commercial context – for instance, if Sanders’ shoes were sold by a fashion brand. In that sense, some archaeologists may see this project as opening a Pandora’s box.

“As soon as we enter the commercial world, then I think for many archaeologists it will be, even though it’s deselected material, an interesting debate ethically,” said Isarin.

“Suppose that all this matter, which has no value at all, that somebody gets rich out of it. That would be a disaster for many archaeologists.”.

Nevertheless, Klaster and Isarin think it is a debate worth having.

Pieces in the exhibition come from practitioners ranging from glass artist Bernard Heesen, working with 17th- and 18th-century glass, to conceptual material designer Shahar Livne, working with mammoth bone, and ceramicist Lotte Douwes, working with Roman pottery.

“We have so much rich material beneath our feet, with amazing stories from 40,000 years up to today,” said Klaster.

The exhibition was previewed at Dutch Design Week, alongside the maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive installation by Maison the Faux and Boris Acket and design collective Show Not Show’s Table of Power exhibition.

It has been revealed that ex Situ: Matter in Translation will be on at See Lab, The Hague, from 5 February to 7 March 2027, with discussion events as part of its programming. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Museum acquisitions round-up: a Simone Leigh monumental bronze and an atmospheric early Rothko

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the American Friends of the National Gallery of Australia bought this sculpture by Simone Leigh last year from Matthew Marks Gallery in Newly introduced York.
  • Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts) (1934) by Mark Rothko.
  • Christopher Rothko, the son of the artist Mark Rothko (1903-70), says that while his father thought “all art was inherently of its time”, sometimes “even with a master of abstraction like Mark Rothko, art can also be inherently of its place”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

National Gallery of Australia, Canberra.

According to recent reports, the American Friends of the National Gallery of Australia bought this sculpture by Simone Leigh last year from Matthew Marks Gallery in Newly introduced York. The monumental bronze, measuring 3.3m long and 1.5m tall, is named after the Nigerian American artist and actress Okwui Okpokwasili. It reveals a reclining woman in a cast raffia skirt, exploring the resilience and cultural memory that merges the semi-abstract female form with the African vernacular. This cast is the second from an edition of two (with one artist’s proof). In 2022, Leigh became the first Black woman to represent the US at the Venice Biennale.

Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts) (1934) by Mark Rothko.

Cape Ann Museum/Christopher Rothko.

Cape Ann Museum, Gloucester, Massachusetts.

Christopher Rothko, the son of the artist Mark Rothko (1903-70), says that while his father thought “all art was inherently of its time”, sometimes “even with a master of abstraction like Mark Rothko, art can also be inherently of its place”. He is referring to this painting—an atmospheric early watercolour-and-gouache work depicting the harbour in Gloucester—which Christopher recently donated to the Cape Ann Museum from his private collection. Mark Rothko frequently summered on Cape Ann, painting alongside two other New York artists: his mentor, Milton Avery, and his friend Adolph Gottlieb. This painting is included in Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea—a touring exhibition presently on view at the Phillips Collection in Washington, DC (until 24 January 2027).

Sources indicate that arc-en-ciel no. 5 (1913-14) by Robert Delaunay.

It may not be instantly recognisable, but the lilac spire behind the rainbow in this painting is the Eiffel Tower—the tallest building in the world when the work was painted by Robert Delaunay (1885-1941). The French artist was the husband of Sonia Delaunay, and in 1912 they co-founded the short-lived Orphism movement—an offshoot of Cubism that prized bright colours and geometric shapes. This vivid oil-on-canvas work, measuring 35cm by 40cm, is one of several variations of the composition and reveals Delaunay moving away from strict geometry to a looser, more expressive and rhythmic style. The painting, which sold at Christie’s in 2025 for $317,500 (with fees) from the collection of Arnold and Joan Saltzman, was exhibited by the London-based dealer Willoughby Gerrish at Tefaf Maastricht in March—where the sale to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, was initially agreed.

Latest Update: Sturdy backs J Cole’s set with neoclassical landmark from rapper’s hometown

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production manufacturer Sturdy.
  • The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.
  • Recent findings suggest that to do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production manufacturer Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

Recent findings suggest that to do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a big part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”.

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that “His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between indicates across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

“That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time highlights were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he stated.

Sources indicate that “We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”.

Recent findings suggest that J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent indicates at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Other set designs recently featured on Dezeen include Dave’s London show, which Stufish illuminated with a laser-shooting piano.

Tech Report: Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears.
  • Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort.
  • Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home. Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up! Why are my ears clogged? Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked: Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage. If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection. Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side. Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too. Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure. Best clogged ear remedies 1. Pop and unclog The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes. 2. Swallow, yawn, or chew The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow. 3. Ear drops Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes. Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful. 4. Warmth and gravity To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily. 5. Hit the steam room Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 6. Take allergy medication Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears. Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort. 7. Rinse away the gunk Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing. When to see your doctor Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention. What not to do when you have clogged ears Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries. Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion. Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation. Takeaway Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies. PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

Recent findings suggest that we're heading into Black Friday evening here in the UK, while our stateside friends are just getting ready to take on the day, but the deals aren't running dry just yet. We're still keeping tabs on the best iPad discounts, including the standard iPad, the Air, the Pro, and the mini, so stick with us to snag the latest steals.

Sources indicate that my favourite deal so far is the Apple iPad Air 11-inch (M4, 2026): was $749 now $649 at Amazon. For a tasty $100, it's a great deal for a powerful iPad that still boasts the lightweight feel of a smaller model like the mini.

It has been revealed that we'll also be sharing tips and tricks, reviews and guides to help you find your perfect iPad match, whether you're a digital artist or an everyday commuter after a lightweight workhorse tablet. And if Apple gear is your thing, our Apple Black Friday deals hub has even more to browse.

Sources indicate that looking for a tablet that covers the essentials, whether that's browsing, streaming box sets, sketching or taking notes? Apple's standard iPad is still a smart buy. It debuted in March 2025 at $349, before Apple lifted the price to $449 in July 2026 as part of a lineup-wide increase. This offer is the cheapest we've seen it since that happened.

Apple's M4 iPad Air only arrived in March, which makes this $100 cut a strong contender for the best Black Friday deal on it. We'd point most buyers here: it costs well under the Pro, yet it supports the Apple Pencil Pro and packs enough muscle for digital painting, photo retouching and the odd Final Cut edit. If you'd like a bigger canvas, the 13-inch version has also dropped by $100.

This is a solid but fairly run-of-the-mill saving on the base 11-inch iPad Pro. The bigger deal is at B&H, where the 13-inch Pro, which earned 4.5 stars from us, is $100 cheaper, and opting for the 512GB model lifts your saving to as much as $150.

Recent findings suggest that if you're after something that can genuinely stand in for a laptop, this tablet is up to the job, with ample power for demanding graphics work and video editing. Its OLED display reaches a peak brightness of 1600 nits for HDR content, and the smooth 120Hz refresh rate keeps everything feeling responsive.

Industry observers note that apple's newest iPad mini only landed earlier this month, so a discount this good, this soon, caught us off guard. Our design editor put it through its paces a couple of weeks back and came away impressed by the latest OLED screen (no other iPad outside the Pro line has one), the quicker A20 Pro chip and the better speakers. Apple Pencil Pro support is still on board as well.

Happy to settle for last generation's 2024 model with the A17 Pro chip and a non-OLED display? Amazon has it marked down to $499.

Another accessory that can unlock an iPad's true potential, especially an iPad Pros, is a good portable SSD drive.

In a recent development, with the standard iPad, you're limited to a max of 512GB internal storage. With the iPad Pros, you can choose up to 2TB. That is a lot of storage space for a tablet, but a 2TB iPad Pro is expensive, and if you're using it as a laptop standing for thinks like editing high-resolution video footage or working on large design projects, it's going to fill up anyway, unless you're working largely in the cloud.

A portable SSD helps you back everything up quickly, you can work directly off the external drive if it's fast enough, and it has more flexibility than internal storage since you can plug it into another device whenever you want.

SSD prices have rocketed this year amid the AI-induced component crunch, so even with Black Friday deals, they're more expensive than what would have been a normal price 12 months ago, but unfortunately these are likely to be the best prices we see for some time.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.
  • In a LinkedIn post, Williamson noted he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.
  • Specifically, he mentioned he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson noted he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he mentioned he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework currently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a latest regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson mentioned his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

Recent findings suggest that “Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”.

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he noted he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

It also proposes new legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

“I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

Recent findings suggest that “While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”.

Industry observers note that williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

According to recent reports, tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:.

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

Industry observers note that these tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:.

In a recent development, tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

According to recent reports, tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

In a recent development, are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s newly introduced best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

According to recent reports, fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Recent findings suggest that tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Industry observers note that flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

In a recent development, keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Industry observers note that furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.

Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.

The organization describes Wild Fig as “a deep, botanical shade with a rich purple tone”, although in certain lights, it looks closer to an earthy oxblood red.

“Full of character and the unexpected, it brings depth and a daring mindset to everyday spaces,” said Abbey Stark, home furnishing direction leader at IKEA US.

Used across furnishings and accessories, it can provide a subtle touch of colour without being overly aggressive, especially paired with warm woods and neutral shades, IKEA US suggests.

But the manufacturer equally pictures it being splashed across entire walls and argues it “unexpectedly fits in” with even brighter colours like baby pink and electric blue – IKEA US’s previous colours of the year.

The tech giant’s Style Guide also pulled out a number of other interior design trends to look out for in 2027, including pattern clashing and Japandi minimalism.

Interior designers have already started making liberal use of Wild Fig, as seen in Note Design Studio’s scheme for the Lammhults showroom in Stockholm, where it blankets walls, floors and ceilings in the entrance, as well as an entire kitchen.

Other predictions for 2027’s colour of the year are set to start rolling in any minute, with Pantone’s set to be unveiled at the start of December.

Paint brand Dulux got ahead of the game when it named a muted green called Soulful Sage as its contender in September.

Some interiors industry insiders, including Dezeen columnist Michelle Ogundehin, have argued at least since the end of the pandemic that “it’s time to reconsider the whole colour of the year carnival”, which was originally invented as a marketing stunt for Pantone’s colour-matching system, much like the Michelin Guide was invented to sell more tyres.

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

#160375. Breaking: ‘Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element’: Yuko Mohri on her exhibition of found objects at London's Barbican

Breaking: ‘Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element’: Yuko Mohri on her exhibition of found objects at London's Barbican

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After picking up the 2025 Calder Prize, the multidisciplinary Tokyo-based Yuko Mohri artist has been on a recent roll, opening institutional highlights from Santander in Spain and her first US solo show in Miami Beach to bringing her 2024 Venice Biennale presentation home to her native Japan.
  • Among the highlights is In Concert (until 24 January 2027), her solo exhibition at the Barbican Centre’s The Curve gallery in London.
  • The Art Newspaper: How did your Barb­ican residency come about?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After picking up the 2025 Calder Prize, the multidisciplinary Tokyo-based Yuko Mohri artist has been on a recent roll, opening institutional highlights from Santander in Spain and her first US solo show in Miami Beach to bringing her 2024 Venice Biennale presentation home to her native Japan.

Among the highlights is In Concert (until 24 January 2027), her solo exhibition at the Barbican Centre’s The Curve gallery in London. At the show’s core is a series of site-responsive kinetic and sound installations made with objects she found at the Barbican. These objects, either stored away or nearly tossed out, embed the history and memories of this famed cultural centre, which will be closed for a year from June 2028 for a £191m revamp ahead of its 50th anniversary in 2032. According to Mohri, the pieces represent an ongoing process that may lead to imperfection, which she finds more profound than a picture-perfect scenario.

The Art Newspaper: How did your Barb­ican residency come about?

Yuko Mohri: When I was approached for a project at The Curve, I discussed with Inês Geraldes Cardoso, the curator of this exhibition, the possibility of researching the Barbican Centre.

Sources indicate that the Curve is a unique and challenging space, and they accept experimental projects with artists. I am not the kind of artist who needs to work within a white cube. I understand why they chose me to create something unique. I am, however, the kind of artist who needs time to understand the environment and identify interesting elements that already exist in that context. A research residency is necessary.

But rather than focusing on just this curved gallery space, I wanted to see what the Barbican really is. It is a huge centre involving many different departments and activities. Thousands of people are also living here in the attached residential complex.

It has been revealed that after rounds of negotiations, I was offered a two-week residency to look for objects and meet the people living and working here. I got a temporary studio at The Pit, a small theatre space located in the basement.

According to recent reports, “Imperfection is everywhere,” Yuko Mohri notes. “It’s a great element.” Photo: © Toby Coulson/Barbican Centre.

What were your biggest discoveries?

The centre has many departments, but they seem very separate from each other and don’t have a lot of communication between them. But since they are going to have a major renovation, they want to revamp the centre’s system, too, and strengthen communication.

We started researching different departments and looked for objects across all the spaces. I wanted to collect objects from here that resonate with the space.

According to recent reports, among the most iconic ones are the original Barbican lamps featured throughout this exhibition. These were once used as street lamps surrounding the centre and also in the building. But as time went on, they were replaced with those of a new design. They were dusty and strange, but I immediately knew that I wanted to use them for my installation. So I spent a lot of time washing these lamps in my temporary studio.

In a recent development, the speakers that I use for the new iteration of the ongoing Decomposition series (begun 2021) located near the entrance to The Curve are old speakers from the Barbican. The found cables that I use to connect the fruit with the lamps and the sound are also very important to me. I also found these metal junk pieces that were discarded in a workshop, and I reappropriated them as triggers for the lamps in the installations in the middle part of the exhibition.

Throughout this project I met many people outside the gallery space, from engineers to the caretakers of the parking space. The extensive communication helped me connect with a lot of open-minded people who accept me and my work.

Yuko Mohri’s Moré Moré (Leaky) is an ongoing installation inspired by the water leaks at Tokyo metro stations Photo: Sun Shi; courtesy the artist, Project Fulfill Art Space, mother’s tankstation, Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tanya Bonakdar Gallery and WHITE SPACE.

How do you relate the centre’s characteristics with your practice?

Recent findings suggest that the Barbican has many water leaks. There’s also a leak of sound because The Curve wraps around the concert hall. So these leaky elements resonate with my practice, especially my ongoing Moré Moré (Leaky) series (begun 2017), which was inspired by the water leaks at Tokyo metro stations and how the staff contain these water leaks with temporary fixes using everyday items. I presented a version of this in Venice.

This time at the Barbican, I created a large-scale installation located towards the exit of The Curve, using found objects such as a pot, an umbrella, plastic bottles, Wellington boots, traffic cones and old water sinks designed for the Barbican apartments.

I also keep the space open and transparent by removing the covers on the entrances and the back so that people can see what’s going on there from the outside. I also exposed the inner layers of the walls to give people a peek into what is behind them.

Are you building an ecosystem within the Barbican that makes the inaudible heard and the invisible seen?

Instead of building, I see it as repairing. Inspired by attending concert rehearsals at the Barbican, I chose the title In Concert, which mirrors the Latin root consertare. It carries the meaning of repair and adjustment, resembling the process of making an organisation.

In a recent development, the process is also similar to making an installation. When I started, I had no idea how it would turn out eventually. I constantly make adjustments to the elements of my installations, like a conductor making adjustments to the tempo or the volume of the musical instruments. The title also reflects that what you see is not stable. Water leaks, gravity and the audience’s presence will change even some very tiny elements. It is not a finalised show. It’s an ongoing process.

Would you say that you are in control and at the same time you also let go?

I am a human being and I have a desire for a certain outcome. But somehow, it doesn’t always work. This trial and error process is a very learnable process for me.

We all have our expectations, but our society and environment have become increasingly unstable. For example, this summer Tokyo rained non-stop for a record 36 consecutive days. We need to adjust our lives. It’s also a necessity when we are based in Tokyo, constantly facing natural disasters like earthquakes. Japan has long been isolated, but now we have many immigrants. Our society is changing. I see this as a kind of training and accept these changing forces. It’s not necessarily about making things perfect. Imperfection is everywhere. It is a great element.

An edition of Mohri’s ongoing installation Decomposition from 2022 in Kanazawa, Japan Photo: Yuu Takagi; courtesy the artist, Project Fulfill Art Space, mother’s tankstation, Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tanya Bonakdar Gallery and WHITE SPACE.

Education: 2004 BFA, Tama Art University; 2006 MFA, Tokyo University of the Arts.

Key indicates: 2026 The Bass, Miami Beach; 2026 Yokohama Museum of Art; 2026 Centro Botín, Santander; 2025 Pirelli HangarBicocca, Milan; 2024 Japan Pavilion, Venice Biennale; 2023 14th Gwangju Biennale.

Represented by: Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, Fresh York; Yutaka Kikutake Gallery, Tokyo; Mother’s Tankstation, London; White Space, Beijing; Project Fulfill Art Space, Taipei.

• Yuko Mohri: In Concert, Barbican Centre, London, until 24 January 2027.

Tech Report: What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns.
  • Recent findings suggest that each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build.
  • Whether you’re in the throes of a latest romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Recent findings suggest that each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a latest romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

Industry observers note that from those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:.

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

In a recent development, research reveals that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

According to recent reports, hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the problems head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

In a recent development, every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

Tech Report: Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1427 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.
  • An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.
  • Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in newly introduced directions.”.

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” remarked the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture.

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” said Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that she saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

“I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she said. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”.

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually become established among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an important influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

After graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” remarked Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”.

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

In a recent development, “We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” mentioned Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

In a recent development, “Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… travelling the world as much as we can to see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”.

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Sources indicate that alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its considered eclecticism.

“We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he mentioned. “I would say it’s something that’s very important and it gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”.

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”.

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell in size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.

Looking ahead, the architects remarked their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo noted there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process, which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”.

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto remarked if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”.

Industry observers note that “If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”.

It has been revealed that to celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

Denver Design District’s rebrand is the ultimate love letter to creativity

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that denver Design District has unveiled a slick upcoming brand identity, transforming the once exclusive design commerce hub into a fresh cultural destination.
  • While there's no formula for creating the best rebrands, Denver Design District's new identity shines in its attention to detail, honouring its rich design heritage while embracing a newfound playfulness.
  • Created in collaboration with D4 Urban and design studio Wunder Werkz, the Denver Design District rebrand centres around a wonderfully contemporary brandmark.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that denver Design District has unveiled a slick upcoming brand identity, transforming the once exclusive design commerce hub into a fresh cultural destination. A blend of design-focused goods, art, retail and food, the new identity marks a more accessible, culturally relevant district made for the masses.

While there's no formula for creating the best rebrands, Denver Design District's new identity shines in its attention to detail, honouring its rich design heritage while embracing a newfound playfulness. Sleek, timeless and characterful, the new brand identity is the ultimate love letter to design.

Created in collaboration with D4 Urban and design studio Wunder Werkz, the Denver Design District rebrand centres around a wonderfully contemporary brandmark. Representing the district's evolution, the 3 'Ds' motif compresses the bold letterforms by a third each time, making for a dynamic visual anchor.

Recent findings suggest that to accomodate the brandmark, Wunder Werkz created DDD Standard, a bespoke midweight sans serif, to act as the district's display typeface. Equal parts "architectural and playful", it draws inspiration from Herbert Bayer's mid-century furniture forms. Paired with an iconographic system of silhouetted design products, clarity and cohesion flow throughout the identity with a confident authority.

Sources indicate that “The idea was to make a more welcoming, accessible district; one that celebrates design in all its forms,” explains Jon Hartman, Partner at Wunder Werkz. “Trade remains an vital part of the ecosystem, but it is no longer the whole story. So, we needed to design a brand that felt open and culturally relevant while still carrying the credibility of the design industry.”.

A rich colour system of brick, blush, slate and deep yellow contrasts the tans and greys of the district's buildings, bringing warmth and personality to the clean design. The result is a refined homage to design that feels accessible and unpretentious, without losing the slick essence of the design district.

Industry observers note that “This project represents the kind of work we love most because it allows us to engage at every level, from strategy and stakeholder alignment through implementation and installation,” adds Hartman. “For us, that’s where the best work happens. Not when design is treated as an afterthought, but when it becomes the link between strategy, space and experience. The result is a brand that feels cohesive at every scale, from a website headline to a warehouse-sized building facade.”.

Industry observers note that “Denver Design District has always been rooted in great design, but our vision for its future is much broader,” notes Dan Cohen, CEO of Denver Design District. “This rebrand isn’t about changing who we are, it’s about reflecting what the District is becoming: a more dynamic, connected, and welcoming destination for Denver and the entire Rocky Mountain region.”.

For more creative inspiration, check out The Royal Albert Hall's majestic rebrand or take a look at the gorgeous McMichael rebrand that's a pure work of art.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Kilian O’Sullivan.

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest latest-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction organization Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design said the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

Industry observers note that “Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”.

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” stated Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he said.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”.

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley mentioned the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The newly introduced development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently announced that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s latest Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”.

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) declared the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising.
  • We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.
  • These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:.

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he claims.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study indicated that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe indicates this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”.

In a recent development, nobbe claims WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he notes.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe claims.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

Brussels’s expansive, €230m Kanal art complex set to open in former Citroën garage

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The much-anticipated Kanal, billed in press materials as Europe’s largest museum development, opens tomorrow (28 November) in a former Citroën garage and showroom on the banks of Brussels’s Charleroi–Brussels Canal.
  • The Brussels-Capital Region acquired the site, which dates back to 1934, in 2015 with the intention of creating a major cultural centre.
  • Sources indicate that three latest structures, called “houses”, have been inserted into the former garage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The much-anticipated Kanal, billed in press materials as Europe’s largest museum development, opens tomorrow (28 November) in a former Citroën garage and showroom on the banks of Brussels’s Charleroi–Brussels Canal. The institution aims to establish Brussels as a major international centre for Modern and contemporary art, and also to provide newly introduced truly public, inclusive institution for the city’s residents.

The Brussels-Capital Region acquired the site, which dates back to 1934, in 2015 with the intention of creating a major cultural centre. The work was then carried out by an international team featuring noAarchitecten, EM2N and Sergison Bates. The resulting complex spans 40,000 sq. m.

Sources indicate that three latest structures, called “houses”, have been inserted into the former garage. Upon entering from the Quai de Willebroeck, visitors find on their left the “Rassembleur”, as the team calls it, which is home to an auditorium and offices. Opposite, on the right, is Kanal Architecture, which is intended to house the CIVA architecture centre and its archives. The transfer of the archives has been delayed following a fire in July. Further along on the right is Kanal-Centre Pompidou, a museum dedicated to modern and contemporary art. This latter space will feature work from the collection of Paris’s Centre Pompidou, with which Kanal signed an agreement in 2017. The agreement, valid until 2031, gives Kanal access to works from the Paris museum's collection, alongside curatorial expertise and support with exhibitions and programming.

More than 20,000 sq. m within the broader Kanal project is devoted to freely accessible public space. The complex also includes creative studios, observation points, a rooftop bar, a bakery, a restaurant and Carrosserie (French for bodywork), a bistro whose counter is made from shaped car-body sheet metal, finished with a chameleon-effect paint. Work on the site is complete, though construction related to the redevelopment of Place Sainctelette surrounding it is still under way and scheduled to continue until the end of 2027.

Industry observers note that the run-up to Kanal’s opening has not been without controversy and challenges. Kanal’s managing director, Yves Goldstein, declared earlier this year that he would step down and he is due to leave his position on Monday (30 November). A statement from the Brussels-Capital Region, the executive body that established the museum, noted in September: “The parties acknowledge a difference of opinion regarding the future of Kanal.” His replacement is yet to be announced.

Recent findings suggest that there have meanwhile been years of debate over the institution’s cost, funding and institutional partnerships. The initial investment budget of €150m (€125m for the works and €25m for studies), set out by the Brussels-Capital region in 2017, rose to around €230m. In May 2026, the region granted the Kanal Foundation, established in 2017 to operate the institution, a €60m loan to help complete the construction works and ensure the museum could open as planned. The budget provided for the ongoing operating of the museum, initially projected at €35m a year, was reduced to €28m in 2026 and is projected to fall to €24m in 2027, €22m in 2028 and €10m in 2029. Brussels’ regional government has previously told The Art Newspaper that private investors will be needed from 2028.

The five-year partnership with the Centre Pompidou will cost around €2m a year. Critics have questioned the expense and the decision more generally of partnering with a Paris institution rather than with Brussels-based organisations. Regional politician Benjamin Dalle has described Kanal as a “top-down political project”, arguing that it should have started with local artists and communities. The Fédération des arts plastiques has raised concerns about the place of Belgian artists in the programme, acquisitions and support for emerging practitioners. Kanal has been approached for comment.

Redzisz, however, has defended the museum’s role as a cultural resource for Brussels and its community. “This museum has an obligation to speak as much to locality as to contribute to global debate,” she told The Art Newspaper in October. That approach is reflected in Kanal–Centre Pompidou’s main inaugural exhibition, in which loans from Centre Pompidou mix with others from international institutions as well as works from the Kanal Foundation. The foundation has a particular focus on contemporary artists connected to Belgium—such as Sammy Baloji, Edith Dekyndt and Aglaia Konrad.

It has been revealed that the show, titled A Truly Immense Journey, features 350 works across three levels. Marcel Duchamp’s Boîte-en-valise, lent by a Belgian private collector, is placed in dialogue with a version of Alberto Giacometti’s L’Homme qui marche I. Kader Attia’s Untitled (Ghardaïa) (2009), a model of a city made from couscous, borrowed from Tate, is shown alongside two portraits of Leonie Ngoie, a Belgian woman of Congolese descent, photographed by the Belgian artist Chrystel Mukeba against an Art Nouveau backdrop by the Belgian architect and designer Victor Horta.

An installation view of A Truly Immense Journey, featuring 350 works across three levels.

Other exhibitions and projects are spread across the Kanal-Centre Pompidou house. No Show, orchestrated by the Brussels-based artist duo Deborah Bowmann and musician Maoupa Mazzocchetti, brings together around 20 artists from the Belgian capital, all of whom are under 40. Clémentine Deliss’s Department of Traps features 70 objects and paintings, including nets, snares, decoys and trompe-l’œil works, deriving from 11 Brussels museums.

Otobong Nkanga’s installation in Hall 2 encourages audience involvement.

A key part of the museum’s strategy is to involve the public directly in its programme. The Antwerp-based Nigerian artist Otobong Nkanga, for instance, has created an installation of wooden looms in Hall 2, inviting participants to weave together and contribute to a collective work of art. Nearly 200 pupils from four neighbouring schools have, meanwhile, contributed to writing exhibition labels. “Inclusivity is the best way for the public to make the place their own,” Kasia Redzisz told The Art Newspaper in January.

By 2030, Kanal expects to attract 550,000 visitors a year.

Breaking: Estudio A-G uses colour to update 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City
