General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

"How did young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?"

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it’s possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.
  • Industry observers note that the last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in Newly introduced York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught.
  • During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it’s possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan.

Industry observers note that the last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in Newly introduced York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught. How had these young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?

During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume.

Having assumed these conversations had become an expected part of design education, I was taken aback by how little the students cared. Instead, they were far more concerned with securing and keeping jobs in an increasingly precarious industry.

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience.

“How do you expect us to make any difference if this is how the industry works?” one asked. Another just wanted to know how to earn a living, without upsetting their employers.

According to recent reports, these were excellent questions, particularly as designers now compete with artificial intelligence capable of executing instructions at extraordinary speed. If design is reduced to following briefs and producing outputs, what space is there for a designer to effect any structural change?

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience. Designers are trained to solve problems, yet rarely encouraged to question who defined them, whose interests they serve, or whether they should exist at all. They are commissioned to make products more sustainable without questioning production volumes, or improve services without examining the policies that make them inaccessible.

It has been revealed that I often say design is a series of well-informed decisions. Every object, building and service emerges from decisions about resources, labor, budgets and the conditions of life.

In a recent development, designers participate in these decisions, although they rarely control all of them. So where does their power begin and end?

Recent findings suggest that imagine a design studio commissioned by a city to address extreme heat in a low-income neighborhood. The brief requests solar-powered cooling shelters and shaded public spaces, with a fixed budget and deadline.

According to recent reports, during research, the designers discover that the proposed shelters would be too far from elderly residents most vulnerable to heat, while existing community centers could accommodate cooling facilities at a lower cost. What should they do? Follow the brief, collect their fees and pretend their hands are tied? Refuse the commission, leaving another studio to complete the work, perhaps feeling rebellious for a moment?

There is a third possibility. They could show the city why its proposal would fail to reach its intended beneficiaries and present an alternative within the same budget. Working with residents and community organizations, they could identify accessible locations, compare costs and demonstrate how the alternative better meets the city’s objectives.

The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client.

Here we see a tangible expansion of design as a civic responsibility. Designers can use their expertise to bring communities into decisions that affect their lives, improving outcomes while sharing decision-making power.

Sources indicate that and if the city insists on its original proposal? The client controls the budget. A junior designer acting alone may have little negotiating power.

But a studio can incorporate community research into its contracts before work begins, negotiate a paid investigation phase and require the client to review evidence and alternatives before approving the design. Of course, this doesn’t guarantee agreement, but it makes critical inquiry a recognised part of the commission.

Sources indicate that design is a practice of applied imagination: understanding interconnected systems to intentionally shape the conditions of life. In this example, designers would examine the relationships between urban planning, public health, housing, energy and community governance. Their value lies partly in identifying what the original commission overlooked and developing viable possibilities with the people affected.

Thanks to the work of people like Victor Papanek, Tony Fry, Ezio Manzini and Arturo Escobar, by now it’s well understood that design has the capacity to shape the world but remains complicit in ecological and social destruction. The challenge today is to translate that knowledge into professional authority, economic leverage and meaningful participation in the decisions that will determine our collective futures.

Recent findings suggest that likewise, advocates of participatory design have long argued for involving people affected by design decisions. The difficult part is to make these commitments part of everyday practice, rather than optional gestures dependent on a sympathetic client.

According to recent reports, meeting these challenges requires rethinking design education. Designers need to learn to investigate the historical conditions behind a problem, understand ecological and economic relationships, and work alongside communities to develop alternatives.

Design can shape community-owned infrastructure, food systems and forms of local governance as well as products and buildings. These are tangible fields of work requiring collaboration and shared authority.

We should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone.

Recent findings suggest that of course, clients may refuse evidence, and insecure workers cannot always risk confrontation. Already there is too much pressure on Gen Z to save the world; we should not ask young designers to compensate for structural failures through personal bravery alone.

In a recent development, studios, educators and commissioners must create paid roles and decision-making processes that give designers genuine influence. What if, for example, investigating the risks and assumptions behind a brief became an essential professional service, one that designers were commissioned and compensated to provide?

Recent findings suggest that I keep thinking about those students at SVA, afraid of being considered difficult. We have taught them how to execute decisions without adequately preparing them to participate in making them. If designers are to take responsibility for their role in shaping the systems that govern our lives, they need a say in the decisions that produce those systems.

In the near future, success would mean residents gaining influence over where public money goes, with designers helping turn their priorities into lasting changes in public planning. This is design as a civic responsibility, and a meaningful distinction from machines optimized to execute instructions. To design possible futures, we must grow the agency designers hold, and the collective power they can help communities to build.

In a recent development, céline Semaan is a Lebanese-Canadian designer, artist, writer, educator and speaker based in New York City, whose work focuses on climate complications and social justice. She is the founder of Slow Factory, a non-profit education and research platform that teaches about regenerative design. Her writing has appeared in The Cut, Vogue, Elle, Refinery29 and New York Magazine, among others. Her first book, A Woman Is a School, was published in 2024. Her upcoming book, Designing Possible Futures, explores the issues discussed in this article, and is due for publication in 2027.

Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

📅 31 Aug 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cutting back on calories but not losing weight?
  • Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight.
  • The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”.

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research highlights starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

It has been revealed that evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:.

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

In a recent development, however, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

In a recent development, so what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Sources indicate that choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Industry observers note that weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That mentioned, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

Carlo Ratti and AI assistant to curate Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism 2027

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Italian architect Carlo Ratti has been named the curator of next year’s Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism, for which he aims to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach.
  • Taking place from 24 September 2027, the biennale will be used by Ratti as an opportunity to question the role of a curator today through the lens of architecture.
  • However, the event’s title, theme and full curatorial team will not be unveiled until 8 December.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Italian architect Carlo Ratti has been named the curator of next year’s Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism, for which he aims to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach.

Taking place from 24 September 2027, the biennale will be used by Ratti as an opportunity to question the role of a curator today through the lens of architecture.

However, the event’s title, theme and full curatorial team will not be unveiled until 8 December.

What Ratti has revealed so far is that he prepares to take “an unconventional, AI-based” approach to the event.

Specifically, he will use an AI assistant, aiming to challenge traditional approaches to developing exhibitions by highlighting emerging tools that can help curators.

“I am delighted to take on the direction of the Seoul Biennale and to explore the future of cities together with the Seoul Metropolitan Government,” says Carlo Ratti.

“Seoul is perhaps the best place in the world to ask how artificial intelligence and the collective wisdom of its citizens might shape the city together,” he continued.

“At the upcoming pre-biennale event, we will begin to introduce the people who will join us, and I think there will be a few surprises – one assistant curator isn’t even human!”.

Ratti is an Italian architect and engineer, and director of his eponymous studio Carlo Ratti Associati. He is also a professor at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

He was appointed by Seoul mayor Oh Se Hoon, succeeding British designer Thomas Heatherwick, who curated the 2025 event.

Heatherwick centred the event on a long, four-storey-high wall displaying images that reflected the ideals of his Humanise campaign.

The Seoul Biennale was established in 2017 by the Seoul Metropolitan Government as a festival of international architecture and urbanism.

“The Seoul Biennale is a place where architects and citizens from around the world think together about the future of cities and explore fresh possibilities,” said mayor Oh.

“Together with general director Carlo Ratti, who has connected architecture, cities, and technology, we will prepare so that the sixth Seoul Biennale offers a new perspective on cities and architecture and a meaningful experience for citizens.”.

Ratti’s previous curatorial experience includes the Venice Architecture Biennale in 2025, for which the theme was Intelligens. Natural. Artificial. Collective. It explored how architecture can be adapted to increasingly unstable living environments through cross-disciplinary collaboration.

At the time, Ratti mentioned, “Dezeen killed the traditional form of the biennale“.

The architect’s other recent projects include the French Pavilion at Expo 2025 Osaka and a proposal for a children’s hospital housed in a one-kilometre “green ring”.

#160287. Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago.
  • Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not upcoming, though it is gaining in popularity.
  • Sources indicate that over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—major and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not upcoming, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

Sources indicate that over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

Industry observers note that for some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

“It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” states Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Sources indicate that patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting latest collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is quickly becoming the preferred method.

“[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” indicates Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

This type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” indicates Dr. Pearl.

Sources indicate that dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

It has been revealed that this is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

Sources indicate that try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

Sources indicate that for cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

According to recent reports, but will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” indicates Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

According to recent reports, if you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

According to recent reports, if injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a blueprint to minimize your pain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Joas Souza.

UK studio RSHP has revealed its first project in the Baltic region, a mixed-use office building in Lithuania designed as “a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking”.

Named after the Lithuanian word for paperclip, the seven-storey Sąvaržėlė is located in central Vilnius, between the UNESCO-listed Old Town and the city’s commercial district.

The stacked building has a cantilevered design and houses office space, a conference hall, a restaurant and a cafe across its 19,000-square-metre space.

“At Sąvaržėlė, we wanted to create a workplace that extends into the city – one that welcomes people, encourages collaboration and contributes upcoming public spaces to Vilnius,” RSHP associate director Jack Evans-Newton said.

“Occupying a unique position between the historic centre and the city’s emerging business district, the building brings these two identities together through a calm and contemporary architectural expression,” he continued.

“Clarity of form, generous public spaces and carefully crafted detailing create a landmark that is unmistakably forward-looking, reflecting the ambition of a growing business district while respecting the scale and character of its historic setting.”.

Sąvaržėlė has large, adaptable floorplates, designed to create a flexible interior.

The building has a stacked, rectangular shape and was made from prefabricated steel components that were bolted together on site. On the east and west facades, RSHP placed external ribs that the studio noted “echo the tones” of Vilnius’ historic architecture.

According to recent reports, sąvaržėlė is arranged around a central glass atrium with a striking yellow-lined elevator. It can be accessed via a number of different entrances that connect to the surrounding streets.

To enhance the building’s environmental performance, RSHP added a double-skin facade. This uses energy-efficient chilled beam cooling and automated natural ventilation to help reduce energy demand.

In addition, Sąvaržėlė has a 2,897-square-metre fully landscaped green roof.

RSHP has also recently designed a 45-storey skyscraper in Shenzhen and a curved-roof railway hub.

Photography by Joas Souza.

What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one problem keeps coming up: the side effects.
  • To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet.
  • But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one problem keeps coming up: the side effects. As notable as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she claims. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”.

Recent findings suggest that fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen says.

You can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen says. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

Fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing issue worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen notes: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

Now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation issue), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen says.

It has been revealed that with that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen claims. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

Industry observers note that people who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we stated above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen states. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”.

It has been revealed that another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

Industry observers note that whatever latest fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu notes. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

Meet BC Architects & Studies & Materials, Marina Tabassum's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, two of BC Architects & Studies & Materials’ founders discuss how their ideas have gone from being perceived as the product of “young idealism” to being taken seriously by the construction sector.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, two of BC Architects & Studies & Materials’ founders discuss how their ideas have gone from being perceived as the product of “young idealism” to being taken seriously by the construction sector.

The Brussels-based studio is at the forefront of bio-regional and circular design, with a whole arm of its practice dedicated to the development of newly introduced materials, often making use of construction waste.

Recently, the studio worked with UK studio Assemble and circular design lab Atelier Luma to create Le Magasin Électrique at Luma Arles in France, with a palette that included everything from rammed earth and construction waste to salt and algae.

Alongside these likeminded practitioners, BC Architects & Studies & Materials is at the forefront of a recent wave of interest in bio-based materials and vernacular methods – ideas that the studio has been championing for some 15 years, pushing for systemic change in the industry.

Founded between 2009 and 2012 by Ken De Cooman, Wes Degreef, Nicolas Coeckelberghs and Laurens Bekemans, the origins of BC Architects & Studies & Materials were – as its tripartite name suggests – not particularly conventional.

The studio is comprised of three different legal entities: BC Architects, an architecture cooperative; BC Studies, a non-profit “education laboratory”; and BC Materials, a material production co-operative.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s approach and outlook was borne out of a series of early projects in Burundi, Morocco and Ethiopia – where the studio briefly had a satellite office – which were grounded in working with local communities and materials.

In a recent development, “A lot of our first experiences in architecture were linked to different construction cultures,” said De Cooman. “I lived in Ethiopia for five years, others were in Morocco for a long time, and at the same time, we were finding our way in Belgium.”.

Recent findings suggest that “It was a different path to learning architecture as a practitioner,” he continued. We learnt to work with local materials and short supply chains, to make do with what you find around.”.

The studio’s first built project was the Library of Muyinga in Burundi, developed using an open-source template from the OpenStructures network and constructed from compressed earth bricks alongside members of the local community.

It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials also designed several school buildings and a women’s shelter in Morocco, often using the construction process itself as an opportunity for the sharing of knowledge around vernacular construction techniques and materials.

According to De Cooman, however, this strand of the studio’s work was never intended to be long-term.

Challenging a tendency in the industry to view these methods and techniques as solely belonging to the realm of “humanitarian” architecture, BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s aim was to apply them to the business-as-usual processes of architecture and construction back home in Belgium.

“It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture,” said De Cooman.

“It was a huge learning process, and now we’re really focussing on the here and now because it’s here that we need to actually change the most.”.

While a big part of this change is the studio’s use of alternative materials, it was also based on the idea of building being an opportunity for shared learning, driven by BC’s belief in the the need for architects to be more engaged with the construction process.

We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other field.

Several of the studio’s early projects in Belgium the result of these learning workshops. Maison de Chasse, a rammed-earth hunting house, was constructed over the course of the first rammed earth workshop in Belgium, based on the techniques of Martin Rauch and Anna Heringer.

In 2017, the renovation of a series of warehouses in Ghent into an artist’s studio for Pascale Marthine Tayou was achieved via a five-week “Urban Construction Camp”, in which volunteers created a newly introduced hempcrete structure inside an existing metal shell.

“We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other fields, not on paper, but with the heart and the hands included,” explained De Cooman.

“It is crazy that we now have a system where, as an architect, you draw all the execution files and send them to a contractor to execute it exactly how you drew it.”.

“The magic happens when everyone can get together – you can draw it together, find a passionate contractor to make it with.”.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials was keen, however, to not be defined by this smaller-scale work, with the whole point being to demonstrate how these techniques and materials could be scaled up into larger contexts.

The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to substantial contractors and buildings.

A key means to achieving this was the formal establishing of BC Materials in 2018, enabled by the interest generated by their earlier projects. Alongside consultancy, workshops and training, the BC Materials arm also offers its own range of earth and clay products, Léém.

“The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to major contractors and buildings,” states Wes Degreef.

“I think we were very surprised that the idea of working with a certain bioregion and its materials is something that we forgot in Europe.”.

Sources indicate that “Some of it still exists, but you really have to search for it. And with earth materials, for example, those crafts don’t exist anymore in Belgium. So we had to do it; we became the craftsmen.”.

Sure enough, the scale of the projects involving BC Architects & Studies & Materials – whether they are engaged as architects or as craftspeople – is growing.

“In the beginning, we were just like young, crazy people who are doing these weird things on Belgium,” said De Cooman.

Recent findings suggest that “There was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium.”.

Industry observers note that there was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium.

In Brussels, BC Architects & Studies & Materials worked alongside EVR-architecten to convert a former barracks into the Usquare Feder university district, the materials for which were sourced in part by the dismantling of several neighbouring buildings.

With numerous other residential and office projects in the works – including a newly introduced bioregional materials hub and workspace in the centre of Brussels, Stadsatelierdeville, that will be its future office.

If it at times felt like BC Architects & Studies & Materials were up against the world, it is projects like La Magasin Électrique, which was a finalist for the 2026 Mies van Der Rohe Award, that reveal a growing international network who share their outlook, one that De Cooman is quick to credit with a lot of their own success.

“I think the dial is shifting, but I don’t think it is us who did it,” remarked De Cooman.

“There are all kinds of practises, organisations, material developers, and so on, who see a different construction sector – it’s a wave, a societal shift.”.

Industry observers note that “We’re very happy about it, but it’s broader than our practice. The construction sector is very conservative and we’re not there yet at all.”.

Degreef adds that external social and economic pressures have also had a hand in forcing change to some degree.

“After Covid and the impacts on material prices, the gap between contemporary materials and the materials we want to promote is not so big anymore.”.

Asked if there is a particular type of building that represents a dream project, however, they remain resolutely focused on processes and systems.

It has been revealed that “I think, for us, it’s not in the buildings itself. It’s not what we build, but how we build and how everybody needs to build.”.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

"Europe's largest museum development" opens in 1930s Citroën garage in Brussels

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Brussels‘ former Citroën Garage has been transformed into Kanal, a 40,000-square-metre museum for modern art and architecture with an exhibition programme developed with the Parisian art institution Centre Pompidou.
  • The transformation was designed by Atelier Kanal, a consortium made up of architecture studio EM2N, NoAarchitecten and Sergison Bates Architects, with a team of construction workers, who restored the 1930s industrial building and added three new volumes within its structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that photography by Koen Van Damme unless otherwise stated. Video by Eyes–Screen.

Brussels‘ former Citroën Garage has been transformed into Kanal, a 40,000-square-metre museum for modern art and architecture with an exhibition programme developed with the Parisian art institution Centre Pompidou.

The transformation was designed by Atelier Kanal, a consortium made up of architecture studio EM2N, NoAarchitecten and Sergison Bates Architects, with a team of construction workers, who restored the 1930s industrial building and added three new volumes within its structure.

Claiming to be “Europe’s largest museum development”, Kanal – sometimes referred to as Kanal-Centre Pompidou – hopes to provide space for people to gather to enjoy visual art, performance, dance, music, film and architecture.

Opening to the public on 28 November, the canal-side building was originally built in 1934 as a garage and showroom for the car company Citroën.

Atelier Kanal aimed to keep the industrial character of the building by implementing a “light touch” approach, restoring most of the building fabric, repairing and upgrading parts where needed, and replacing other parts to improve climatic and acoustic conditions.

The garage’s former showroom, a modernist curved glass building with 20-metre-tall interiors, was converted into a gallery space topped with a publicly accessible rooftop.

“Rather than a spectacular gesture, our proposal offers an attitude of ‘radical optimism’ – open and non-prescriptive, spontaneous and instinctive – much like the spirit of modern progress in which it was created,” said Atelier Kanal.

“The interior is a fine example of elegant industrial engineering, while the glass facades clearly express early modernism,” it continued.

“Our ambition has been to trust the building as we found it, embracing its industrial character and many layers of use.”.

Three latest buildings were added inside the existing structure, including a four-storey volume with a basement level that contains art galleries, and another volume housing a 378-seat auditorium and the Kanal offices.

The third volume is the upcoming home for Brussels’ museum and archive of architecture, Kanal Architecture, which was formerly known as CIVA.

Rising nine stories on the north-east side of the campus, across from the art galleries, the structure includes exhibition spaces, a library, archives, research centre, bookshop and workshop spaces.

Architecture collective Assemble designed an indoor playground on the first floor of the museum, which features playscapes informed by volcanoes, planets, and piles of coal that were once transported on the canal.

Elsewhere in the building are a library, bookshop, rooftop bar, restaurants and an in-house bakery.

Kanal’s year-round programme of exhibitions was developed in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou art museum in Paris.

“Kanal invites citizens, organisations, collectives and communities to appropriate and inhabit large parts of the building, for production, performances, events, informal gatherings or simply to spend time,” said Atelier Kanal.

Sources indicate that “The museum extends beyond curated art, becoming part of the city and its fabric,” it continued. “In this sense, Kanal departs from the traditional museum and instead offers a place for civic gathering, responding to the growing absence of shared public spaces in our cities today.”.

Other museums that have recently opened in historic buildings include the London Museum, located in a transformed Victorian market building, and a bank in Santander that was transformed into the Faro Santander museum.

Photography by Koen Van Damme unless otherwise stated. Video by Eyes–Screen.

Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility.
  • Industry observers note that the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol.
  • According to recent reports, that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a newly introduced reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

Industry observers note that the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”.

According to recent reports, that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”.

But is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Industry observers note that our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a massive deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Recent findings suggest that beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

According to recent reports, despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson claims. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”.

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

Sources indicate that but logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial issues that occur with age, Dr. Molina claims. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”.

As with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson indicates. It’s also extra vital to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

Sources indicate that there’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she indicates—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

This precision begins with a careful reading of the existing context, including the recognition of the spatial, material, and environmental conditions that shape a place. It extends into the process of design and construction, where complex considerations are distilled into deliberate, coherent decisions. Rather than pursuing formal complexity or reduction for its own sake, a measured intervention seeks to establish a meaningful relationship between what already exists and what architecture can contribute.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Design agency Base Design has created a more compact version of credit card firm Visa’s logo and worked with Displaay Type Foundry on a fresh typeface, as part of a refresh of the brand’s visual identity.

While the 2021 Visa wordmark remains unchanged, the refresh included creating a shortened symbol for the brand, rolling out the newly introduced Visa Sans typeface, and creating a blocky hero graphic to market towards a younger generation.

“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition – it’s relevance,” said Base Design executive creative director Min Lew.

“Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the next generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”.

As part of this strategy, the studio cut the V out of the existing wordmark to function as its own symbol. It will be used on credit cards and appear across digital platforms.

The studio also wrapped it in colourful bar, which will also be used on graphic elements such as posters, and to frame text.

“More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity,” mentioned Lew.

“This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences.”.

For Visa Sans, Base Design and Displaay Type Foundry also based the design on the existing logo.

The typeface features rounded edges akin to the rounded corner of the Visa V, and overall, extends “the logo’s character across the wider identity”.

Ultimately, the newly introduced identity was created to be used across different smaller, touchpoints according to the team, such as at tap-to-pay stations, at checkout, or online, as the brand appears “for only a moment” in day to day life.

According to recent reports, “We have deep trust and recognition as a brand,” mentioned Visa chief marketing officer Frank Cooper III. “This refresh gives us an opportunity to build on that.”.

A more subtle approach to logo and branding updates has been popular in recent years, such as at Walmart and Google.

In contrast, the US restaurant chain Cracker Barrel recently took a hard swing at a logo patch, which was immediately met with online backlash and promptly scrapped in favour of the original design.

Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone.
  • It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body.
  • Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

Recent findings suggest that but retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next massive thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Recent findings suggest that retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” indicates Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”.

The medication is presently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide owners lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an matter that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

Sources indicate that “Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”.

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”.

Sources indicate that that includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

Sources indicate that but, with all medications, Dr. Ali claims it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel states. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

If you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali claims. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more notable, he points out.

Photography by Daniel Reiser.

The UK’s Royal Society for Arts has confirmed five Royal Designers for Industry, who include Durrell Bishop and Bridget Baines, as well as naming an Honorary Royal Designer as it celebrates its 90th anniversary.

The awards, which were established in 1936, recognise outstanding talent across landscape architecture, technology, illustration, fashion and theatre. They are given by Royal Society for Arts (RSA) and can only be held by 200 designers at any one time.

This year’s winners are product and interaction designer Bishop, multidisciplinary designer Harris Elliott, illustrator Laura Carlin, costume designer Tahra Zafar and landscape architect Bridget Baines.

Baines co-founded international practice Gross Max, and her fellow Gross Max founder Eelco Hooftman (pictured in main image with Baines) was given the Honorary Royal Designer award this year.

The winners were chosen for their “joyful” designs,.

Industry observers note that “Ninety years on, the Royal Designers are still looking forward,” Keeper of the Faculty of Royal Designers for Industry Johanna Gibbons said. “This year’s appointments show how far design now reaches, from public landscapes and picture books to exhibitions, the stage and the objects we use every day.”.

“Their work is joyful, and it is serious about making life better,” she continued. “That is what unites Royal Designers across the decades: a living entanglement of disciplines that, with the RSA Fellowship, is a profound force for good.”.

Last year’s winners included designer Yinka Ilori and journalist Mona Chalabi, and the award has also been given to designers including Es Devlin, Vivienne Westwood, James Dyson and Zandra Rhodes.

According to the RSA, the winners represent the “sheer breadth of design today”.

“Great design changes how we experience the world, often in ways we barely notice,” RSA programme manager Catherine Joyce.

“For 90 years, Royal Designers have shown what extraordinary creativity can achieve, and how it can make life better for everyone,” she continued.“These six appointments are a wonderful reminder of the sheer breadth of design today.”.

Dezeen also recently celebrated the best designers of this year as part of our Dezeen Awards, including Ilori, Yasmine Ghoniem and Keiji Ashizawa.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spanish lighting brand Marset has showcased five of its products on Dezeen Showroom, including a mid-century reissue and a ceiling light that appears like a block of ice.

Marset‘s selection includes the Gambosa table lamp, created by designer Mathias Hahn to reinterpret the classic shade, stem and base as one smooth, glossy sculpture in steel and opal polycarbonate.

Gambosa is defined by its elegant composition, with a round-ended body that looks as if precariously balanced. It also features a considered cable design that sweeps down one side of the lamp like a signature.

It is distinguished by its select palette of colours, with combinations of orange, moss grey, black, pale pink and opal that evoke mid-century style combined with contemporary curation.

With the Lauro collection, Marset has revived a genuine 1970s design classic from its own catalogue, featuring chunky tubes of bent steel.

In a recent development, created by designers P Aragay and J Pérez Mateo, the Lauro lighting comes in table, floor and wall variants. According to Marset, the range represents the technical achievements of a time when bending steel was a huge challenge.

Another of the highlights from Marset is the Ringo lighting, crafted by designer Joan Gaspar from transparent polycarbonate that is rotomoulded, giving it a dimpled texture reminiscent of a melting block of ice.

Available in flush-mounted or pendant styles, the design has a simple cylindrical shape, with scale and materiality bringing fresh life and visual impact.

Another of Gaspar’s designs is Domus, an angular bollard-style outdoor light that, through simple gesture, recalls a warmly lit house at night.

Industry observers note that the design is available in three heights. Units can be optionally combined to create a sculptural look and the illusion of multiple windows.

Geometric glass volumes, metal detailing and glowing bar-shaped lighting elements meet in the Fragile collection, designed for the brand by Jaume Ramírez.

The lights come in pendant, wall and table formats, each made up of spherical and conical shades that lend them a playful aesthetic.

The roots of the Marset brand stretch back to the 1940s, when Francisco “Paco” Marset established a small metal foundry in Barcelona.

His grandchildren Javier and Carlos Marset helped reposition the company as the global design brand it is today when they took over in the 1990s, bringing on board designers such as Gaspar, who is a frequent collaborator.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Video by Jim Stephenson.

An old Victorian infirmary transformed into an educational space by UK studio Bennetts Associates has won the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland for 2026.

Named the Edinburgh Futures Institute, the project involved refurbishing the Category A-listed structure, originally designed by Scottish architect David Bryce, and integrating newly introduced teaching and work spaces for the University of Edinburgh.

The Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) noted the award jury praised the project for its “modern, welcoming, clever and stimulating” design that successfully blends “Scottish Baronial architecture with modern innovation”.

“The Edinburgh Futures Institute stood out for its civic generosity, scale and ambition,” said RIAS president Libby Heathcote, who is associate director at Reiach and Hall Architects.

“Balancing loyalty to David Bryce’s diagram with creativity in introducing bold new interventions is a remarkable achievement, blending historic Scottish Baronial architecture with modern innovation,” she continued.

“The result is a modern, welcoming, clever, and stimulating place that people want to work in and return to.”.

Central to Bennetts Associates‘ redevelopment was the restoration of the building’s existing fabric, which was at risk of dereliction after being vacated in 2003.

Updates to the existing structure included reopening an original clock tower and public plaza, as well as the restoration of original wards and 150-metre-long corridors.

Across its five floors, flexible teaching and work zones were added alongside upcoming public areas such as exhibition space and a 450-seat event hall below ground.

Sources indicate that the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual prize named after Scottish architect Andrew Doolan, who passed away in 2004. It recognises buildings of all typologies.

Sources indicate that the Edinburgh Futures Institute was chosen as this year’s winner ahead of two other adaptive reuse projects. These have each been featured in a series of videos produced by Jim Stephenson and published by Dezeen and RIAS to showcase the shortlist.

The other two projects shortlisted were the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by London-based Studio Octopi and the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture.

Previous winners of the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland award include the Union Terrace Gardens by Stallan-Brand and LDA Design and the Burrell Collection museum by John McAslan + Partners.

Video by Jim Stephenson.

Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation.
  • Industry observers note that the study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected.
  • “These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But new research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

Industry observers note that the study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

“These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

The research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

The researchers discovered that while participants remarked they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

“We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh claims. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”.

People are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

As a result, Dr. Gallagher says she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”.

Industry observers note that these chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

Recent findings suggest that “Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen notes. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a significant impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen says.

Over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan notes. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

Of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan notes. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”.

Industry observers note that ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she claims. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
